'''''Anthurium clarinervium''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Araceae]] native to [[Chiapas]], [[Mexico]]. The ''[[Anthurium]]'' genus is known to contain approximately 1,000 species, resulting in one of the most diverse Central American tropical plant genera.<ref name=dist/>

== Description ==
''A. clarinervium'' is a deep forest green colored plant with a velvety leaf surface, with reticulate venation which is an uncommon venation pattern for a [[Monocotyledon|monocot]]. The veins vary between ivory and light green in color and are usually 1 cm in width.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Thekkayam |first1=Sabina |title=Ornamental Plants |date=2009 |publisher=New India Publishing Agency |location=India |isbn=9788190851268 |id={{isbnt| 8190851268}} |pages=150 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZaN2LfUt2oAC&q=anthurium%20clarinervium |access-date=30 October 2021}}</ref> It has ovate, deeply-lobed leaves, resembling a love heart, with whitish veins,<ref>{{Cite book |title=Aroids : plants of the Arum family |last=Deni. |first=Bown |date=2000 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=0881924857 |edition=2nd |location=Portland, Or. |pages=311 |oclc=43499544}}</ref> atop stems that are 1–2 cm thick. It grows naturally as an [[epiphyte]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=Ornamental plants |last=George. |first=Thekkayam, Sabina |date=2009 |publisher=New India Pub. Agency |others=Peter, K. V. (Kuruppacharil Varkey), 1948- |isbn=9788190851268 |location=New Delhi |pages=150 |oclc=427744226}}</ref> ''A. clarinervium'' produces orange berries containing numerous seeds and reproduces via [[Sexual reproduction of plants|sexual reproduction]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2021-08-04 |title=Anthurium Crystallinum vs Clarinervium: 3 Main Differences |url=https://www.greengardentribe.com/anthurium-crystallinum-vs-clarinervium-3-main-differences/ |access-date=2021-12-06 |website=Green Garden Tribe |language=en-us |archive-date=2021-12-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206050533/https://www.greengardentribe.com/anthurium-crystallinum-vs-clarinervium-3-main-differences/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This species has been unofficially placed in the category of Esqueleto herbs (Esqueleto is Spanish for skeleton), as the veins of the leaves resemble a ribcage.<ref name=":0" /> It is similar in appearance to and may be confused with [[Anthurium crystallinum|''Anthurium'' ''crystallinum'']].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anth. clarinervium |url=http://www.aroid.org/TAP/species/anthclairnerv.php |access-date=2021-12-06 |website=www.aroid.org |archive-date=2021-09-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920220620/http://www.aroid.org/TAP/species/anthclairnerv.php |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Distribution ==
[[File:Anthurium clarinervium 2zz.jpg|thumb|'''''Anthurium clarinervium'' spadix'''<ref>source: David Stang. First published at ZipcodeZoo.com</ref>|252x252px]]
''Anthurium clarinervium'' tends to grow in wet disturbed forests or elevated cloudy environments.<ref name=dist>{{cite journal |last1=Croat |first1=Thomas |title=The Distribution of Anthurium (Araceae) in Mexico, Middle America and Panama |journal=Selbyana |date=October 1986 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=94–99 |url=https://journals.flvc.org/selbyana/article/view/120796 |access-date=3 November 2021 |jstor=41888790 |archive-date=6 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206182536/https://journals.flvc.org/selbyana/article/view/120796 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is found naturally in Mexico. ''Anthurium clarinervium'' is an aroid [[Perennial plant|perennial]] that flourishes in shaded regions of Mexico’s limestone ledges.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Korniichuk |first=Serhii |title=Anthurium - How to Grow and Care - for Beginners and Professionals |publisher=Independently published |date=November 30, 2020 |isbn=979-8573735306 |pages=3–18 |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
''A. clarinervium'' was first discovered in the 1950s in a small region of southern Mexico, growing at an elevation of {{convert|2500–3800|ft|m}} It was found in a [[karst]]ic rainforest region in soil containing limestone.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |title=Anthurium Clarinervium {{!}} Plant Care Guide |url=https://urbanhouseplant.com/anthurium-clarinervium-matuda-care/ |website=Urban Houseplant |access-date=13 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206035630/https://urbanhouseplant.com/anthurium-clarinervium-matuda-care/ |archive-date=2021-12-06}}</ref> This type of ''Anthurium'' is found thriving off other plant's nutrients through water absorption from other plants. ''A. clarinervium'' also absorbs different nutrients from leaves and debris from the rain.<ref name="auto"/>

== Cultivation ==
Although it grows naturally in tropical climates, many people find it to have attractive qualities, resulting in a high demand as a house plant.<ref>{{cite web |title=The story of Anthurium |url=https://www.fusionflowers.com/section.php/1546/1/the_story_of_anthurium |website=FusionFlowers Magazine |access-date=9 November 2021}}</ref> This plant exists in both a horticultural environment and in a tropical, natural environment. People enjoy the look of this species because it can bloom for several months and because of its unique foliage. ''Anthuriums'' can be challenging as houseplants because it is not easy to match the conditions of their natural environment in houses. But because an ''Anthurium'' is an epiphyte, they can survive many different habitats that are not similar to their normal humid rainforest environment.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Knight |first1=Tom |title=Anthurium Houseplants |url=https://www.ourhouseplants.com/plants/anthurium |website=ourhouseplants.com |publisher=our houseplants.com |access-date=10 November 2021 |archive-date=6 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206034115/https://www.ourhouseplants.com/plants/anthurium |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Chiapas in Mexico (location map scheme).svg|thumb|252x252px|''Anthurium clarinervium'' occurs in Chiapas, Mexico]]
Bright, indirect sunlight is required for this plant. It prefers temperatures from low {{convert|70|F|C}} to low {{convert|80|F|C}}, and humidity at 50% or higher, optimally 75-85%. The plant do not do well in small amounts of light, and veins can then lose saturation. It also does not do well in direct sunlight, which may cause burns on foliage. Modest fertilization is necessary for this plant to flourish. Aerated and loose soil is desired, with moderate levels of moisture.<ref name=":0" /> ''A. clarinervium'' will struggle to grow in thick clay soil, with possible root rot. Soil pH between 5.5 and 6.8 is ideal.<ref name=":1" />

== Toxicity ==
''Anthurium clarinervium'' is poisonous to both humans and common pets upon ingestion. Toxic harm results from the presence of [[calcium oxalate]] crystals in the leaves which can cause improper mineral absorption and inflammation of the lining of the digestive tract. Ingesting this plant can cause drooling, nausea, trouble swallowing or breathing, diarrhea, and pain in the mouth and throat. Remedies include removing all parts of the plant, and rinsing out mouth with either milk or water. The calcium in the crystals and milk will bind together and reduce pain.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Seeds |first1=Evergreen |title=Anthurium Clarinervium {{!}} Complete Grow and Care Guide |url=https://www.evergreenseeds.com/anthurium-clarinervium/ |website=www.evergreenseeds.com |access-date=December 5, 2021 |archive-date=November 30, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130192912/https://www.evergreenseeds.com/anthurium-clarinervium/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Diseases ==
The genus ''Anthurium'' is susceptible to multiple types of bacterial and fungal diseases.

=== Bacterial diseases ===
* Bacterial blight (''[[Citrus canker|Xanthomonas axonopodis]] pv. dieffenbachiae)''- Forms easily visible water-logged lesions along the leaf. Leaves also begin to yellow and necrosis occurs. Bacteria enters via pores or wounds such as rips, tears, or punctures. 
* Bacterial wilt (''[[Ralstonia solanacearum]])''- Typical wilting symptoms are observable with this disease. Plant exhibits leaf yellowing and stem browning. Vascular system allows swift spread of disease. Ooze or slime may leak out of wound of infected plant.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=PP292/PP292: Anthurium Diseases: Identification and Control in Commercial Greenhouse Operations |url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/PP292 |access-date=2021-12-06 |website=edis.ifas.ufl.edu |language=en |archive-date=2021-12-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206193517/https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/PP292 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Fungal diseases ===
* ''Rhizoctonia'' root rot (''[[Rhizoctonia solani]])'' – Stems, typically young ones, become water-logged and droop due to the increased weight. The root system is also attacked.
* ''Phytophthora''/''Pythium'' (''[[Phytophthora nicotianae]]'' var. ''parasitica'' and ''[[Pythium splendens]])'' – Both fungi are considered [[oomycete]]s, otherwise known as water molds, and attack the root system. Wilting, [[chlorosis]], and root dieback are all common symptoms. 
* Black nose disease (''[[Glomerella cingulata|Colletotrichum gloeosporioides]])'' – As the name suggests, the floral [[Spadix (botany)|spadix]] forms black spots, which rapidly grow and may result in spadix death.<ref name=":2" />
